explanation: Fires at full strength only on a '0' inside a long run of repeated zeros (e.g. '0000000[[0]]', zero-padded numbers or timestamps). Everything else it touches (repeated-digit strings, 'aspx', word pieces) stays near 10% or below with no shared theme.

Fires broadly at 80-100% on a wide variety of tokens: function words ('the', 'by', 'of'), technical subword pieces ('array', 'ethylene', 'ly'), code tokens and wiki boilerplate ('External links'). I can't find a shared lexical or contextual trigger, so I can't predict its strength on new text.

Fires on tokens near the start of a news or report sentence, especially when it introduces a recent event or date: 'asked for', 'Recent', 'a new report', month or weekday names, fiscal-year digits, and license boilerplate such as 'This program is'. Strongest in journalistic or announcement prose; weak in ordinary text.

A mixture. It fires on the subword 'bol' (bolus, Bolin, bolts, boliviensis), on code and markup punctuation in key-value or tag contexts (',' after clientId, ' :' in Ruby hashes, ' <', '"></'), on the '/c' and '/D' slash-joined pieces, and on assorted other tokens.

Fires on assorted tokens with several apparent sub-patterns: the '+' after a negative leading term in generated math polynomials ('-v**3 + v**2'), 'You will' in instructions, 'to' after 'relative'/'closest', and code tokens such as '#define fi first' and 'before :each'. There is no single unifying theme.

Fires on a mixed set: digits inside long numbers (prime-factor outputs, figures), quantifier words in Chinese or Vietnamese ('tất cả', 'mọi', '的情况下'), code identifiers ('bsobj', 'HKLM', '.Data') and ordinary English words. I see no common thread.

Fires most strongly on a separator token right after a long run of repeated identical characters, such as ' +' after '000000000' (timezone offsets like +0800), ',' after '8888', or a run of ';' after ';;;;'. Elsewhere it gives only weak activation (about 20%) on scattered subword pieces of names and technical words.

Fires on the second or later subword piece of a multi-token word or a fixed compound term, especially in boilerplate or technical text: 'Lymph-ob-lastic', 'rounded corners', 'THE COPYRIGHT HOLDERS', 'AWS account', 'non-ref-und-able', 'Monday-F-riday'. The token completes a predictable phrase or word.

Fires on the second digit of a multi-digit number (for example '4' in '44.5%', '3' in '5,376', '4' in port '5432'), especially where the digit is hard to predict, as in percentages, counts and ports. Non-numeric tokens give only weak to moderate activation.

Fires on the adjective or determiner right after 'the', 'a' or 'an' that picks out a place or option in phrases like 'the right place', 'a desired location', 'the only one', 'the correct place', 'a particular place', 'among other cities' and 'from all over'. It is strongest when the noun that follows is a place or location.

Fires on backslash tokens. These include namespace or registry path separators ('ORM\ManyToOne', 'HKLM\Hardware', 'Monolog\Handler'), escape sequences ('\n', '\r'), LaTeX or Doxygen backslashes, and especially the ' \[' that begins an escaped citation ('\[@CR1') at the end of a scientific sentence. Other code punctuation gives weak activation.

Fires on a heterogeneous set: the end of rare words split into pieces ('table-aux', 'Boliv-arian', 'L-STM', 'Pepperd-ine'), 'you' in 'brought to you' or 'inform you', line breaks in legal document headers, and 'h' in 'k'th term'. There is no clear single theme.

Fires on content-word tokens or subwords that begin or continue a compound or technical term ('Per-man-ently', 'birth-place', 'car-box-y', 'equ-inox', CJK characters in compounds like '移設' and '新入社員'). It spans many languages and topics without a clear unifying cue.

Fires on tokens in rigidly formatted header or boilerplate text. It is strongest on court-document captions ('UNITED STATES', 'IN THE', 'FOR THE TENTH', middle initials in names next to 'Clerk') and on namespace or package path pieces in code ('NHapi.Base', 'Mage_Sales', '.boost'). Usually the text is heavily indented or structured.
